seoTitle: Free Unicode Character Inspector and Lookup Tool
metaDescription: Inspect any character: code point, category, script, UTF-8 and UTF-16 bytes, HTML, JS and CSS escapes. Free, handles emoji, runs in your browser.
intro: Paste any characters and get the code point, general category, script, UTF-8 and UTF-16 bytes and the HTML, JavaScript and CSS escapes for each one.
why:
Some text looks right but behaves wrongly: a hyphen that is really a minus sign, a space that does not break, an invisible character inside an identifier, a Latin-looking letter that is actually Cyrillic. You cannot see these differences, but your search, sort, regex or database comparison can.

This inspector breaks a string into characters and reports what each really is. You get the U+ code point, its Unicode category, its script, the encoded bytes, and ready-made escapes for HTML, JavaScript and CSS. Non-printing characters are labelled as such. The first 100 characters are analysed, entirely in your browser.
howTo: Paste or type the characters you want to identify. Up to 100 are analysed.
Read the block for each character: code point, category, script and encodings.
Check the Emoji line if you are unsure whether a symbol is treated as emoji.
Copy the HTML, JS or CSS escape you need.

faq.a: It checks a practical list: Latin, Greek, Cyrillic, Armenian, Hebrew, Arabic, Devanagari, Bengali, Thai, Georgian, Hangul, Hiragana, Katakana, Han, Common and Inherited. Anything else is labelled "other".

faq.q: Why does a flag or family emoji give several results?
faq.a: Those are sequences of several code points joined together. The inspector lists each code point separately, which is useful for seeing the joiners and regional indicators inside them.

faq.q: How do I find invisible characters in my text?
faq.a: Paste the text and look for entries marked "(non-printing)" or categories starting with Z or C, such as Format or Control. The Zero-width Detector scans for these automatically.

faq.q: Is this a full Unicode database?
faq.a: No. Category, script and emoji data come from your browser's own Unicode property support, so results depend on its Unicode version. Character names are not included.
